implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance, so a decorator is a wrapper type that owns the inner value and implements the same trait, forwarding each method explicitly - the compiler enforces the full forwarding obligation. Make the inner type a generic parameter (`struct Counting<W> { inner: W }`) and every layer monomorphises to static dispatch, which is exactly what std::io does: BufReader 'adds buffering to any reader' and is itself a Read, so BufReader<GzDecoder<File>> composes with no vtable and no boxing. Switch the field to Box<dyn Trait> only when the chain is assembled at runtime from configuration, accepting a heap allocation and a virtual call per layer, and never implement Deref to fake automatic forwarding - the API guidelines reserve Deref for pointer-like types, and it lets calls bypass the added behaviour.
idiom_name: generic newtype wrapper implementing the same trait and forwarding (BufReader/BufWriter shape); Box<dyn Trait> for runtime-assembled chains
pitfalls: Generic stacking changes the type at every layer, so a function cannot name the composed type - return impl Write, box the chain, or introduce a type alias at the seam; Box<dyn Write> is the escape hatch, not the default.
Trait methods with default implementations are silently not forwarded unless overridden or explicitly delegated, and the wrapper then uses the default behaviour instead of the inner value's.

Sharing a decorated service across threads needs Send/Sync bounds and Arc; interior mutability must live inside the wrapped value (Mutex/RwLock) or the wrapper needs &mut self, which changes the call sites.
